messages.subject: About fitting random slope model and using half-t prior
messages.subject_clean: About fitting random slope model and using half-t prior
messages.body_plain:
Hi developer team,

Happy holidays and thank you for the great maintenance of the package all this time.

I have a question regarding fitting random slope models. Code as below:
HT.prior = "expression:
sigma = exp(-theta/2);
nu = 3;
log_dens = 0 - 0.5 * log(nu * pi) - (-0.1207822);
log_dens = log_dens - 0.5 * (nu + 1) * log(1 + sigma * sigma);
log_dens = log_dens - log(2) - theta / 2;
return(log_dens);
"
h.t = list(prec = list(prior = HT.prior))

model <- inla(outcome ~ State + TxARM + f(State, TxARM, model = "iid",
                                          , hyper = h.t,
                                          constr = TRUE),
              data = sample_data,
              lincomb = lc,
              family = "pom",
              verbose=FALSE, control.compute = list(config=TRUE))

I want to use half t distribution for my hyperparameter(hierarchical variance of state variable). There are two levels for State and 2 levels for TxARM. However, I got error as attached. I am wondering if I am specifying my model wrong or if there is any other problem.

Another question is, I am wondering if it is possible to specify a scale parameter for the half t distribution (so specifying both scale and degrees of freedom). I could not figure out a proper way to do so.

Thank you in advance and have a great day!

Best,
Jocelyn

                    hyper = h.t,
                    constr = TRUE),

              data = data.frame(outcome, State, TxARM, State2 = State,
TxARM2 = TxARM),
              verbose=FALSE, control.compute = list(config=TRUE))

well, you need to rename State as you can only use it once...

messages.subject: seasonal model: standard deviation of the seasonal random effects
messages.subject_clean: seasonal model: standard deviation of the seasonal random effects
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I fitted a spatiotemporal (bym + seasonal) model with four years of disease data (2016-2019)
to investigate the factors associated with and predict seasonal disease incidence.

Then, I
used this model to predict seasonal incidences for the years 2020 and 2021. It
seems that the prediction uses the mean of the spatial and seasonal random
effects from 2019. However, the standard deviation of the seasonal effects of 2020 and 2021 increased a lot compared to the standard deviation of those seasonal
effects from 2016-2019 (about 6 to 11 times higher for 2020 and 2021, respectively).
See the figure below.

Can you
please tell me why the model is doing this?  It seems to produce a large variability in the
predicted incidence.

Thank you
very much for your time and your help!

Regards,

Wen

messages.body_plain:
the behaviour looks kind of ok to me.

its all about how regular each season is... you can test it out with
this code

slen <- 4
n <- 4*10
eta <- sin(2*pi * 1:n/(slen+0.2))
s <- 0.2
y <- eta + rnorm(n, sd = 0.1)
y[n:(n-2*slen)] <- NA
r = inla(y ~ -1 + f(idx,
                    model = "seasonal",
                    scale.model=TRUE,
                    season.length = slen),
         data = data.frame(y, idx = 1:n),
         control.family = list(hyper = list(prec = list(
                                            initial = log(1/s^2),
                                            fixed = TRUE))))
plot(r)

messages.subject: Implausibly high random effect from iCAR logistic regression
messages.subject_clean: Implausibly high random effect from iCAR logistic regression
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I am fitting a relatively simple logistic regression with an iCAR (3,033 observations, with 6.5% 1's). But this model returns implausibly high and skewed random effect variance estimates. I would be very grateful for advice on diagnosing the root cause of this?

Reprex (data available on request, as I can't seem to post it here)

library(INLA)
library(spdep)
reprex_df_1 <- readRDS(file = "reprex_df_1.rda")

###  Define neighbours ###
naighbour_matrix  <- poly2nb(reprex_df_1)
nb2INLA("Analysis.graph", naighbour_matrix)
Analysis.adj <- paste(getwd(), "Analysis.graph", sep ="/")
Analysis.Inla.nb <- inla.read.graph(filename = "Analysis.graph")

### Fit a model with one fixed effect and the iCAR ###
formula_1 <- PACTO_01 ~ T_sp_km2_level + f(ID,  model = "besag",  graph = Analysis.Inla.nb,  adjust.for.con.comp=TRUE, scale.model=TRUE,   constr = TRUE)
Model_1 <- inla(formula_1, family = "binomial",  data = reprex_df_1,  control.compute = list(dic = TRUE, waic = TRUE))

prec <- Model_1$summary.hyperpar
var <- 1/prec

Many thanks

### Approach suggested by Blangiardo and Cameletti to get the odds.
library(ggplot2)

# How many areas?
Nareas <- nrow(Model_1$summary.random$ID)

# Extract the marginal posterior distribution for each element of the random effect
csi <- Model_1$marginals.random$ID[1:Nareas]

# Apply the exponential transformation and calculate the posterior mean for each of
# them using the lapply function.
zeta <- lapply(csi, function(x) inla.emarginal(exp,x))

# Add to DF
zeta_DF <- do.call("rbind", zeta)
reprex_df_1$zeta <- zeta_DF

# Plot
p2 <- ggplot() +
  geom_sf(data = reprex_df_1, aes(fill = zeta), colour=NA) +
  guides(fill=guide_legend(title="Posterior mean for\nthe random effects (odds)")) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low='#a50026', mid="#ffffbf", high='#006837')

messages.subject: strange behaviour in simple model
messages.body_plain:
As an example for how to write R-inla commands I generated the following data

set.seed(1)
m<-100*20
x<-rnorm(m)
area<-sample(seq(1,20),size=m,replace=T)
#parameter values
#random effect precision
tau.v0 <- 2
tau.v1 <- 1.5
#fixed effect
b0 <- 5
b1 <- 2
#overall precision
tau <- 3

v0 <- rnorm(length(unique(area)),mean=0,sd=(1/sqrt(tau.v0)))
v1 <- rnorm(length(unique(area)),mean=0,sd=(1/sqrt(tau.v1)))
#allocate the area effect to each observation
v1j<- v1[area]
v0j<- v0[area]

#y with a random intercept + slope model
#generate y with mean the model and some variance
y <- rnorm(m, mean=(b0+v0j)+(b1+v1j)*x, sd=(1/sqrt(tau)))

#make a data frame to pass to inla
ris.data<-data.frame(y=y, x=x, area=area)

I then put a very basic model with a random intercept and fixed slope

ri.formula <- y ~ 1 + x + f(area, model="iid")

ri.inla<-inla(ri.formula,
              family="gaussian",
              data=ris.data)

Then I look at the results:

round(ri.inla$summary.fixed[,c(1:3,5)],3)

sometimes (even with the same value for set.seed) I get sensible results but most of the time I get really high values for the sd of the fixed effects. What is going on? I feel I am missing something fundamental.

Running R 4.2.2.

Thanks,
Sara

messages.body_plain:
I think the model is not well defined as you have two terms fighting
against each other, the 'area' and the 'gaussian noise', and you need to
tell what you want/believe in the priors for these two precisions. f.ex
that 'area' should be contracted to variance=0, like here

ri.formula <- y ~ 1 + x + f(area, model="iid",
hyper = list(prec = list(
prior = "pc.prec",
param = c(1, 0.01))))

messages.subject_clean: Computational bottleneck for large n, but low-dimensional latent field
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am fitting a multivariate spatial model with three responses, x (Gamma), y (Gamma),  and z (Bernoulli). The number of spatial locations is large (n ~ 1,000,000), but the range of the spatial effects is large relative to location density, so I can use a low-dimensional latent fields (k = mesh$n ~ 2,500).

Vector x is fully populated, but y and z and many missing values (NAs), with around 20,000 entries populated and the rest NAs.

The goal of the analysis is to get posterior means and sd's for y and z at all of the locations, including the NAs. Actually, I eventually want posterior means and sd's of y*z, but perhaps I'll cross that bridge next.

If I truncate my observations/locations to only complete observations across x, y, z with the same mesh (so n ~20,000, but still k ~2,500), the analysis is very fast, completing in around 10 minutes. But if I include all values, the analysis is very slow. I only attempted it once, and my laptop crashed after over 8 hours of runtime. I am running with 'verbose = T', and strangely the longest stage is the preliminary stage, before inla() starts printing out gradients, likelihood evaluations, etc. The text it pauses on is:

Strategy = [DEFAULT]
    Mode..................... [Classic]
    Sparse-matrix library.... [taucs]
    OpenMP strategy.......... [huge]
    num.threads.............. [4:1]
    blas.num.threads......... [1]

It sat here for multiple hours. This huge difference in runtime contradicts my knowledge of INLA, as I thought the primary bottleneck was Cholesky's of k x k precision matrices, and k has not changed. I have set quantiles = NULL and control.predictor(quantiles = NULL) to try to avoid any unnecessary computing there.

Any thoughts on the computational bottleneck here? Things I can do to speed it up?

Below is the R code for the INLA infrastructure. Thanks in advance.

#############################
me = 0.4
mesh = inla.mesh.2d(loc.domain = coord, max.edge = c(me, 5*me)
                    , offset = c(me,6*me)
                    )
mesh$n # around 2,500

A = inla.spde.make.A(mesh, coord)

spdey = inla.spde2.pcmatern(mesh = mesh,
                           prior.sigma = c(2, 0.01),
                           prior.range = c(1, 0.01))

spdex = inla.spde2.pcmatern(mesh = mesh,
                            prior.sigma = c(1.2, 0.01),
                            prior.range = c(1, 0.01))

spdez = inla.spde2.pcmatern(mesh = mesh,
                           prior.sigma = c(3, 0.5),
                           prior.range = c(1, 0.01))

stacky = inla.stack(data = list(Y = cbind(y, NA, NA), link = 1),
                    A = list(A),
                    effects = list(list(inty = 1, s1 = 1:mesh$n)))

stackx = inla.stack(data = list(Y = cbind(NA, x.hat, NA), link = 1),
                    A = list(A),
                    effects = list(list(intx = 1, s12 = 1:mesh$n, s2 = 1:mesh$n)))

stackz = inla.stack(data = list(Y = cbind(NA, NA, z), link = 1),
                    A = list(A),
                    effects = list(list(intz = 1, s13 = 1:mesh$n, s3 = 1:mesh$n)))

stack = inla.stack(stacky, stackx, stackz)

form = Y ~ 0 + inty + intx + intz +
  f(s1, model = spdey) +
  f(s12, copy = "s1", fixed = F) +
  f(s2, model = spdex) +
  f(s13, copy = "s1", fixed = F) +
  f(s3, model = spdez)

mod = inla(formula = form, family = c("Gamma", "Gamma", "Binomial"),
           data = inla.stack.data(stack),
           control.predictor = list(A = inla.stack.A(stack),
                                    link = link,
                                    quantiles = NULL),
           control.inla = list(strategy = 'gaussian', int.strategy = 'eb'),
           quantiles = NULL,
           verbose = T)

messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA discussion group,

I recently had to switch from HPC and I have been facing issues in running R INLA since then.  Given the available modules/libraries and the user rights, I have no choice but to use Conda environments.

I managed to successfully install R 4.2.2 and R INLA (latest test version, binary build for Centos7) but the working example from the website yields the following error message:

sh : ligne 1 : 4684 Instruction not allowed (core dumped) '/home/supplisson/.conda/envs/RINLA/lib/R/library/INLA/bin/linux/64bit/inla. mkl.run' -s -v -t16:1 -B0 -P compact '/tmp/RtmpJRNCI0/filef977153d4cd/Model.ini' > '/tmp/RtmpJRNCI0/filef977153d4cd/Logfile.txt'.

I don't think there is any issue with my R installation per se since I get no error when installing/loading R INLA (I have tried multiple times) and basics examples for rjags and bmrs/stan are working. However, if this can be of any help, I installed these packages through the Conda command and R-INLA directly through install.packages (the last version on Conda is 2 years old).

Has anyone had a similar problem before and could give me a hand? I am a beginner in HPC/Linux so I may have missed an easy fix.

Cheers,
Olivier

messages.body_plain:
You can use either 'table:' or 'expression:', see

inla.doc("table:")

this is the example for precision ~ Gamma(a,b). you need to change the
below, and add the Cauchy prior, or what the prior is for the precision
is std.dev <http://std.dev> is cauchy.

I think Cauchy is a waaaaay to heavy tailed and exponential on std.dev <http://std.dev>
is more sensible, which is the pc prior for precision, use
prior="pc.prec". just my opinion

prior.function = function(log_precision) {
    a = 1;
    b = 0.1;
    precision = exp(log_precision);
## CHANGE HERE
    logdens = log(b^a) - lgamma(a) + (a-1)*log_precision - b*precision;
## END OF CHANGE HERE
    log_jacobian = log_precision;
    return(logdens + log_jacobian)
}

lprec = seq(-10, 10, len=1000)
prior.table = paste(c("table:", cbind(lprec, prior.function(lprec))),sep
= "", collapse = " ")
n = 100
y = rnorm(n)

r = inla(y~1,
         data = data.frame(y),
         control.family = list(
             hyper = list(
                 prec = list(
                     prior = prior.table))))

messages.subject: informative gamma priors for the precisions in the hierarchical rw1 model
messages.subject_clean: informative gamma priors for the precisions in the hierarchical rw1 model
messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA-experts,

Could you please suggest how to introduce informative gamma priors for the precisions in the hierarchical random walk plus noise model?

For example, the attached picture ("1101-1") shows the fitted values from such a model. I want to decrease overfitting and make “fit.0.025quant” and “fit.0.975quant” (somewhat) wider.

Could you guys please suggest how I should change the code below so as to alter a Gamma prior on the precision of a rw1 model and decrease precision for the id.b0 effect?

I have attached the code, data and the initial results.

Julian Faraway on his website https://julianfaraway.github.io/brinla/examples/rbd.html  lists one possible suggestion for that. I have tried to implement it in this example, but it didn’t help

Code:

g <- n_distinct(data$group)
n <- n_distinct(data$id.b0)

re.b0 <- rep(1:g, each = n)

data <-
  cbind.data.frame(
    data,
    re.b0
  )

formula <- response ~ -1 +
  f(id.b0,
    model = "rw1",
    constr = FALSE,
    replicate = re.b0)

model <- inla(
  formula,
  data = data,
  control.predictor = list(compute = TRUE),
  control.compute = list(
    dic = TRUE,
    waic = TRUE,
    cpo = TRUE,
    config = TRUE
  )
)

fit.model.H1 <- model$summary.fitted.values
fit.model.H1$group <- data$group

obs.fit.model.H1 <-
  cbind.data.frame(data[, c(1, 3, 2)], fit.0.025quant = fit.model.H1[, c(3)],
                   fit.0.975quant = fit.model.H1[, c(5)], fit.mean = fit.model.H1[, c(1)])

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Excessive memory use for regression model
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Excessive memory use for regression model
messages.body_plain:
Hi Harvard
I solved the problem by changing the autoregression parameter. It now doesn't calculate AR on each (sometimes sparse) species in every plot, but over all species in a plot. This has shrunk memory needs to ~ 100gb.
I also noticed that some kind of parallelization must still occur, since the models run much faster with threads = 4. I hypothesise that the estimations for each random effect are parallelized, but don't require much memory per CPU. Only when the integration is done, does it require the full 200gb of any CPU.

My institute is not very fast with new software on the HPC, so they have earliest started working on this this week.

In any case, thanks for your help.

Roel

	hyper=list(prec=list(prior="pc.prec",
			     param=c(A,0.1)))

which will give marginal stdev, after integration out the precision, of
0.31*A,

for poisson counts and log-link, I would use A=1 or A=0.5, similar for
binomial

for resons discussed in the pc-prior paper (Stat sci'17), I do not
longer use gamma-priors for precions in applications

messages.subject: vb.correction aborted warning
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I'm running across a new error about limit of vb.corrections being aborted (I have played around with the limit a bit) and was wondering how to interpret it.

I'm running a spatio-temporal model with interactions -- this is for teaching purposes and not because I necessarily believe in this model. I've left all the default priors etc.

The code for the 4 models I'm running is below I've attached most of the output of verbose for one of the models (it wouldn't all fit in the Rstudio output window)  the warning that is generated by the type 2 and 3 but NOT type 1 and 4 models is below.

I'm guessing the vb.correction is related to this paper https://arxiv.org/pdf/2111.12945.pdf and was wondering whether anyone had any idea what is going on and what sensible priors there might be -- if there are any in this situation.

Finally, prior to the latest update in r-inla (and R) the same code was running with a different warning (which I cannot quite remember right now)

This is by no means urgent but I'd be interested in any insights.

Thanks,
Sara

vac.mnth.typeI <- month_doses ~
  #structured spatial
  f(num_id, model="bym", graph=london.adj)+
  #structured time
  f(month, model="rw2") +
  #iid time
  f(month1, model="iid") +
  #interaction
  f(num_id.month, model="iid")

vac.mnth.typeI.inla <- inla(vac.mnth.typeI , family="poisson",
                      data = vac.mnth, offset=log(population),
                      control.predictor =list(compute=TRUE),
                      control.compute = list(dic=TRUE))

#check that there are the right amount of interaction terms
#this should be the number of boroughs (33)
#times the number of months (6)
length(vac.mnth.typeI.inla$marginals.random$num_id.month)

## -----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
#temporal
month.int <http://month.int> <- vac.mnth$month
#spatial
num_id.int <http://num_id.int> <- vac.mnth$num_id

## -----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
vac.mnth.typeII <- month_doses ~
  f(num_id, model="bym", graph=london.adj) +
  f(month, model="rw2") +
  f(month1, model="iid") +
  f(num_id.int <http://num_id.int>, model="iid",
    #iid on the spatial component
    group = month.int <http://month.int>,
    control.group = list(model="rw2"))
# rw2 structure on the temporal component

vac.mnth.typeII.inla <- inla(vac.mnth.typeII , family="poisson",
                      data = vac.mnth, offset=log(population),
                      control.predictor =list(compute=TRUE),
                      control.compute = list(dic=TRUE), verbose=TRUE)

## -----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
vac.mnth.typeIII <- month_doses ~
  f(num_id, model="bym", graph=london.adj) +
  f(month, model="rw2") +
  f(month1, model="iid") +
  f(month.int <http://month.int>,model="iid",
#iid on the temporal component
       group = num_id.int <http://num_id.int>,
    control.group = list(model="besag", graph=london.adj))
# besag on the spatial component

vac.mnth.typeIII.inla <- inla(vac.mnth.typeIII , family="poisson",
                      data = vac.mnth, offset=log(population),
                      control.predictor =list(compute=TRUE),
                      control.compute = list(dic=TRUE))

## -----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
vac.mnth.typeIV <- month_doses ~
  f(num_id, model="bym", graph=london.adj) +
  f(month, model="rw2") +
  f(month1, model="iid") +
  f(num_id.int <http://num_id.int>, model="besag", graph=london.adj,
        #spatial component
    group=month.int <http://month.int>, control.group = list(model="rw2"))
  #temporal component

vac.mnth.typeIV.inla <- inla(vac.mnth.typeIV , family="poisson",
                      data = vac.mnth, offset=log(population),
                      control.predictor =list(compute=TRUE),
                      control.compute = list(dic=TRUE))

the output you attached is screeming for help...

the model needs to contact to simpler ones, otherwise this does not make
sense (to me, at least).

intrinsic priors needs to be scaled, otherwise, effect of priors depends
on the model.

for the poisson I would use

f(..., model="rw2", scale.model=TRUE,
	hyper=list(prec=list(prior="pc.prec", param=c(0.5,0.01)))

and use 'bym2' instead of 'bym'.

use same prior for the iid model

use proper prior for the intercept

messages.subject: variance component with prior specifying non-zero floor
messages.subject_clean: variance component with prior specifying non-zero floor
messages.body_plain:
Assume we have a priori information that a variance component (an "iid" random effect, or anything really) has a plausible range of .2 plus or minus .03.  So, we are virtually certain the value is not zero, but also that it is not particularly large. We want the prior to reflect both parts of this information.

First, am I correct that the pc.prior on the precision would not be a good choice for this application, because (a) it specifically sets only a (soft) ceiling, and (b) the only available floor is zero?

Second, if we want to set a different prior that does reflect this a priori knowledge, say N(.2, .03), how do we account for the fact that the prior apparently needs to be specified on the *log* precision? As such, I assume it is not as simple as taking the reciprocal of the square of the SD. Once I figure out the log transformation portion, hopefully some normal or truncated normal would work fine for this prior as a practical matter, although perhaps there are other options worth considering.

Thank you.

messages.subject: Combining posteriors using model weights
messages.body_plain:
Hi all.

I am doing some analyses with INLA and would like to pool the posteriors for a
parameter value from two competing models, where the two models have different
model weights (based on information criteria, WAIC). I wrote a function to combine
the two posteriors, where the weights determine the number of samples from
each posterior that will be added to the pooled posterior. Does this seem like a
reasonable way to combine posteriors based on model weights? I know there is a
vast literature on Bayesian Model Averaging that might tell me if my hack is reasonable
or not, but I don't have the chops to find the answer in all that vastness.

I pasted the code below in case (1) it is reasonable approach and (2) it is useful to
someone else. Caution to future readers, read the full thread before using this potentially ridiculous code.

Thanks!
Tim

# simple function to create an aggregate distribution based on weights----------
get_weighted_posterior <- function(dists, wts, summa=T, histo=T){
  # get and test inputs
  nposts <- length(dists)
  if(nposts<2) {
    stop(message="ERROR...there is only one distribution.")}
  nsamps <- length(dists[[1]])
  if(nposts<2 | var(lengths(dists))!=0) {
    stop(message="ERROR...lengths of distributions do not match.")}
  nwts <- length(wts)
  if(nposts!=nwts) {
    stop(message="ERROR...numbers of distributions and weights do not match.")}
  samp_mat <- matrix(unlist(dists), nrow=nsamps, ncol=nposts)
  dist_wts <- unlist(wts)
  if(sum(dist_wts)!=1) {
    stop(message="ERROR...weights do not sum to one.")}
  # make a weighted aggregate distribution
  new_dist <- numeric()
  for(i in 1:nposts){
    subsamp <- sample(samp_mat[,i], size=(nsamps * dist_wts[i]))
    new_dist <- c(new_dist, subsamp)
  }
  # create summaries
  summ <- NULL
  if(summa==T){
  summ <- c(mean=mean(new_dist), sd=sd(new_dist),
            quantile(new_dist, probs=c(0.025, 0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.9,
                                 0.95, 0.975)))
  }
  # plot a histogram
  if(histo==T) hist(new_dist)
  # return list
  return(list(weighted_distribution=new_dist, weights=dist_wts, summaries=summ))
}
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------

# function tests ---------------------------------------------------------------
# two test distributions
n <- 100000
mu1 <- 10; sd1 <- 3
mu2 <- 14; sd2 <- 2
y1 <- rnorm(n, mu1, sd1); hist(y1); summary(y1)
y2 <- rnorm(n, mu2, sd2); hist(y2); summary(y2)

# equal weights
get_weighted_posterior(dists=list(y1, y2), wts=list(0.5, 0.5),
                       summa=T, histo=T)$summaries
c(mean=mean(c(y1,y2)), sd=sd(c(y1,y2)))

# all weight on y1
get_weighted_posterior(dists=list(y1, y2), wts=list(1, 0),
                       summa=T, histo=T)$summaries
c(mean=mean(y1), sd=sd(y1))

# all weight on y2
get_weighted_posterior(dists=list(y1, y2), wts=list(0.00, 1.00),
                                   summa=T, histo=T)$summaries
c(mean=mean(y2), sd=sd(y2))
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------

# with inla --------------------------------------------------------------------
# data
n <- 100
x <- 1:n
y <- rnorm(n, (2 + 0.5*x - 0.0005*x^2), 5)
df <- data.frame(x=x, x2=x^2, y=y)
plot(y ~ x)

# two models
library(inlabru)
m1 <- bru(y ~ 1 + x, data=df)
m2 <- bru(y ~ 1 + x + x2, data=df)

# model weights
library(dplyr)
waics <- data.frame(model=c("m1", "m2"),
                        waic=c(m1$waic$waic, m2$waic$waic)) %>%
  arrange(waic) %>%
  mutate(delta_waic=waic-min(waic),
         rel_lik=round(exp(-0.5 * delta_waic), 3),
         waic_wts=rel_lik / sum(rel_lik)) %>%
  pull(waic_wts)

# two sets of posteriors
fun1 = function() {return (Intercept + 50 * x)}
s1 <- inla.posterior.sample(50000, m1)
lc1 <- as.numeric(inla.posterior.sample.eval(fun1, s1)); summary(lc1); hist(lc1)

fun2 = function() {return (Intercept + 50 * x + 50 * x2)}
s2 <- inla.posterior.sample(50000, m2)
lc2 <- as.numeric(inla.posterior.sample.eval(fun2, s2)); summary(lc2); hist(lc2)

# weighted posterior
wt_post <- get_weighted_posterior(dists=list(lc1, lc2), wts=list(waics[1], waics[2]),
                       summa=T, histo=T)
wt_post$summaries

messages.subject: Estimating prior hyperparameters for the Matern auto-correlation
messages.subject_clean: Estimating prior hyperparameters for the Matern auto-correlation
messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA experts,

I want to use a Matern autocorrelation function to model “intrinsic” autocorrelation in the distribution of fish eggs, i.e., the autocorrelation which cannot be explained with any external factor like temperature or water depth. Conceptually, my model of fish egg abundance would be the sum of a deterministic fixed part depending on environmental factors and a random effect explaining only intrinsic auto-correlation:

Response = GLM on environmental factors + random spatial effect    (1)

where the “random spatial effect” would arise from a Matern function with some range and variance (amplitude?). I know that I can let INLA to “freely” find optimal values for these Matern  (hyper)parameters. However, I have good reasons (details omitted for brevity) to give a *fixed* value for the range of the Matern function. I know that I can do this with:

spde <- inla.spde2.pcmatern(MeshA, prior.range = c(range0, Prange), prior.sigma = c(sigma0, Psigma))

where range0 is my estimate of the auto-correlation scale for intrinsic autocorrelation and Prange should be NA. Now these are my questions:

1) How can I get such prior (fixed) estimate for range0 which is consistent with my model (1)? Here is the one possibility I can think of:

1.a) Fit the “GLM on environmental factors” without random effect;

1.b) Estimate an empirical (isotropic) auto-correlation function rho(R) of the model residuals as function of distance R by defining distance classes between the observational points and using some simple estimator of auto-correlation;

1.c) Use the graphic of rho(R) to get an estimate of range0 (e.g., first zero-crossing of rho(R) or half decay from the maximum) or, if we want to get fancy, use non-linear methods to fit the parameters of the Matern function;

1.d) Once range0 is obtained, fit equation (1) with the prescribed Matern function with INLA.

Correct? Are there other options?

2) If I let INLA to freely fit the Matern parameters: how can I know and/or extract the resulting values after the fit (i.e., how to extract the values of the posterior Matern hyperparameters)?

messages.subject: Model parameters change with “predicting” data
messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA experts,

I have noticed that the parameters of my GLMM slightly change in value depending on whether I fit the model only to the observational data or if I include “testing” or “predicting” data points (i.e., the points of my regular grid). Here is what I mean:

I fit my model like this:

-----------------------------------

MODS <- inla(formula = as.formula(FMLAS), data = hydrodata, family = "tweedie",
          control.family = list(hyper =  list(
              theta1 = list(initial = 1.725),
              theta2 = list(initial = -4,
                    prior = "loggamma",
                    param = c(100, 100)))),
             inla.mode = "experimental",
             num.threads = NC,
             verbose = T)

-----------------------------------

where “hydrodata” contains only observations and my model FMLAS is:

-----------------------------------

> FMLAS
[1] "CPUE ~ BATH + log(BATHGRAD):log(sumEP+1) + I(log(BATHGRAD)^2) + TEMP:log(sumEP+1) + I(TEMP^2):log(sumEP+1) + log(sumEP+1) + LON + LAT + I(LON^2) + I(LAT^2)"

-----------------------------------

After fitting, the model parameters are:

-----------------------------------

Fixed effects:
                                mean    sd 0.025quant 0.5quant 0.975quant mode
(Intercept)                  -32.371 6.269    -44.668  -32.370    -20.080   NA
BATH                           0.000 0.000      0.000    0.000      0.001   NA
I(log(BATHGRAD)^2)            -0.062 0.028     -0.118   -0.062     -0.007   NA
log(sumEP + 1)                -3.639 0.699     -5.010   -3.639     -2.267   NA
LON                            0.033 0.056     -0.077    0.033      0.142   NA
LAT                            1.174 0.242      0.700    1.174      1.649   NA
I(LON^2)                       0.001 0.003     -0.004    0.001      0.006   NA
I(LAT^2)                      -0.010 0.002     -0.015   -0.010     -0.006   NA
log(sumEP + 1):log(BATHGRAD)   0.290 0.055      0.181    0.290      0.399   NA
log(sumEP + 1):TEMP            0.583 0.109      0.368    0.583      0.797   NA
log(sumEP + 1):I(TEMP^2)      -0.022 0.004     -0.030   -0.022     -0.013   NA
                             kld
(Intercept)                    0
BATH                           0
I(log(BATHGRAD)^2)             0
log(sumEP + 1)                 0
LON                            0
LAT                            0
I(LON^2)                       0
I(LAT^2)                       0
log(sumEP + 1):log(BATHGRAD)   0
log(sumEP + 1):TEMP            0
log(sumEP + 1):I(TEMP^2)       0

Model hyperparameters:
                                  mean    sd 0.025quant 0.5quant 0.975quant
p parameter for Tweedie           1.70 0.005       1.69     1.70       1.71
Dispersion parameter for Tweedie 19.56 0.314      18.97    19.55      20.21

-----------------------------------

Now let us include also testing points in the fitting procedure, I do this by appending the testing points to the data frame “hydrodata” (see here why: https://www.r-inla.org/faq [ctr F "How can I do predictions using INLA"]):

-----------------------------------
hydrodata <- rbind(hydrodata, climdata)
-----------------------------------

where climdata is a data frame with the same variables as hydrodata, but containing NA for the response CPUE, i.e.:

-----------------------------------
climdata$CPUE <- NA
-----------------------------------

Now, after fitting the model again by calling inla() with exactly the same configuration from above (MODS <- inla...), the model parameters are slightly different:

-----------------------------------

Fixed effects:
                                mean    sd 0.025quant 0.5quant 0.975quant mode
(Intercept)                  -19.277 3.584    -26.307  -19.277    -12.248   NA
BATH                           0.001 0.000      0.001    0.001      0.001   NA
I(log(BATHGRAD)^2)            -0.034 0.018     -0.070   -0.034      0.002   NA
log(sumEP + 1)                -3.182 0.478     -4.119   -3.182     -2.245   NA
LON                           -0.042 0.038     -0.117   -0.042      0.032   NA
LAT                            0.696 0.142      0.417    0.696      0.976   NA
I(LON^2)                      -0.002 0.002     -0.006   -0.002      0.002   NA
I(LAT^2)                      -0.006 0.001     -0.009   -0.006     -0.003   NA
log(sumEP + 1):log(BATHGRAD)   0.245 0.037      0.173    0.245      0.317   NA
log(sumEP + 1):TEMP            0.539 0.074      0.393    0.539      0.685   NA
log(sumEP + 1):I(TEMP^2)      -0.020 0.003     -0.026   -0.020     -0.015   NA
                             kld
(Intercept)                    0

I(log(BATHGRAD)^2)             0
log(sumEP + 1)                 0
LON                            0
LAT                            0
I(LON^2)                       0
I(LAT^2)                       0
log(sumEP + 1):log(BATHGRAD)   0
log(sumEP + 1):TEMP            0

Model hyperparameters:
                                  mean    sd 0.025quant 0.5quant 0.975quant
p parameter for Tweedie           1.74 0.004       1.73     1.74       1.74
Dispersion parameter for Tweedie 39.69 0.456      38.80    39.68      40.59

-----------------------------------

Here are my questions:

1) Why do the model parameter values change with the “predicting” data? For me this makes no sense, since a prediction should be independent of the data used to train the model... Is this dependence of model parameters on the predicting data with INLA correct at all or I am doing or understanding something wrong? In case this is correct, is this some kind of “Bayesian” standard issue, i.e., kind of a concept which does not exist in frequentist statistics?

2) I wonder if it is at all needed to involve the predicting points in the INLA fitting procedure. Why not simply to make a prediction by fitting the model only to the observations and, once the model parameters have been found, *evaluating* the GLM in the predicting points?

Example of what I mean:

-----------------------------------

# Extract the model parameter values:
modparam <- MODS$summary.fixed$mean

# We need now to calculate the “model matrix”, but first,
# we need to indicate R to include NAs in the predictors to obtain
# also Nas in the model matrix (otherwise the model matrix is shorter
# in the missing values):
options(na.action='na.pass')

# Now here comes the model matrix, i.e., a matrix including a column per model
# term (including a column of 1s for the intercept) and each row being the
# model term evaluated in a testing point of “climdata”:
X0 <- model.matrix(as.formula(FMLAS), data = climdata)

# We have to mutiply now the model matrix X0 with the vector of model
# parameter values “modparam” *columnwise*. To do so, we define a
# matrix with the values of modparam in the diagonal and use the
# matrix multiplication operator %*% :
AB_ <- X0 %*% diag(modparam)

# Finally, we add the multiplication AB_ of fitted model
# parameters and model terms evaluated on the testing points and apply
# the inverse link function (in my case, it is a log link):
AB <- exp(as.vector(rowSums(AB_)))

-----------------------------------

Now we have the predicted response stored the variable AB, evaluated on a regular grid. This procedure is identical to what you obtain with the function gam() of mgcv and the function predict(). You can even compute error estimates for the response variable by using the 0.95 credible intervals instead of using the parameter means, i.e. repeat the procedure with:

-----------------------------------
modparam_high <- MODS$summary.fixed$"0.975quant"

modparam_low <- MODS$summary.fixed$"0.025quant"
-----------------------------------

So, why not to use this “evaluation” procedure instead of including the predicting points in the call to inla()? Does it have any disadvantage in comparison? Is this only possible in the absence of random effects? Otherwise:

How to do the “evaluation” procedure when you have random effects? I guess that you can extract the random parameters with MODS$summary.random but: is there also an equivalent “model matrix” for random effects? How to compute it?

messages.body_plain:
Great, thanks Haavard!

On Thu, Jan 19, 2023 at 4:37 PM INLA help <he...@r-inla.org> wrote:
> There is a function
>
> inla.merge
>
> that will combine results with given weight
> On 19 Jan 2023 at 18:51 +0000, Tim Meehan <tme...@gmail.com>, wrote:
> > Hi all.
> >
> > I am doing some analyses with INLA and would like to pool the posteriors for a
> > parameter value from two competing models, where the two models have different
> > model weights (based on information criteria, WAIC). I wrote a function to combine
> > the two posteriors, where the weights determine the number of samples from
> > each posterior that will be added to the pooled posterior. Does this seem like a
> > reasonable way to combine posteriors based on model weights? I know there is a
> > vast literature on Bayesian Model Averaging that might tell me if my hack is reasonable
> > or not, but I don't have the chops to find the answer in all that vastness.
> >
> > I pasted the code below in case (1) it is reasonable approach and (2) it is useful to
> > someone else. Caution to future readers, read the full thread before using this potentially ridiculous code.
> >
> > Thanks!
> > Tim
> >
> > # simple function to create an aggregate distribution based on weights----------
> > get_weighted_posterior <- function(dists, wts, summa=T, histo=T){
> >   # get and test inputs
> >   nposts <- length(dists)
> >   if(nposts<2) {
> >     stop(message="ERROR...there is only one distribution.")}
> >   nsamps <- length(dists[[1]])
> >   if(nposts<2 | var(lengths(dists))!=0) {
> >     stop(message="ERROR...lengths of distributions do not match.")}
> >   nwts <- length(wts)
> >   if(nposts!=nwts) {
> >     stop(message="ERROR...numbers of distributions and weights do not match.")}
> >   samp_mat <- matrix(unlist(dists), nrow=nsamps, ncol=nposts)
> >   dist_wts <- unlist(wts)
> >   if(sum(dist_wts)!=1) {
> >     stop(message="ERROR...weights do not sum to one.")}
> >   # make a weighted aggregate distribution
> >   new_dist <- numeric()
> >   for(i in 1:nposts){
> >     subsamp <- sample(samp_mat[,i], size=(nsamps * dist_wts[i]))
> >     new_dist <- c(new_dist, subsamp)
> >   }
> >   # create summaries
> >   summ <- NULL
> >   if(summa==T){
> >   summ <- c(mean=mean(new_dist), sd=sd(new_dist),
> >             quantile(new_dist, probs=c(0.025, 0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.9,
> >                                  0.95, 0.975)))
> >   }
> >   # plot a histogram
> >   if(histo==T) hist(new_dist)
> >   # return list
> >   return(list(weighted_distribution=new_dist, weights=dist_wts, summaries=summ))
> > }
> > # --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
> >
> >
> > # function tests ---------------------------------------------------------------
> > # two test distributions
> > n <- 100000
> > mu1 <- 10; sd1 <- 3
> > mu2 <- 14; sd2 <- 2
> > y1 <- rnorm(n, mu1, sd1); hist(y1); summary(y1)
> > y2 <- rnorm(n, mu2, sd2); hist(y2); summary(y2)
> >
> > # equal weights
> > get_weighted_posterior(dists=list(y1, y2), wts=list(0.5, 0.5),
> >                        summa=T, histo=T)$summaries
> > c(mean=mean(c(y1,y2)), sd=sd(c(y1,y2)))
> >
> > # all weight on y1
> > get_weighted_posterior(dists=list(y1, y2), wts=list(1, 0),
> >                        summa=T, histo=T)$summaries
> > c(mean=mean(y1), sd=sd(y1))
> >
> > # all weight on y2
> > get_weighted_posterior(dists=list(y1, y2), wts=list(0.00, 1.00),
> >                                    summa=T, histo=T)$summaries
> > c(mean=mean(y2), sd=sd(y2))
> > # ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
> >
> >
> > # with inla --------------------------------------------------------------------
> > # data
> > n <- 100
> > x <- 1:n
> > y <- rnorm(n, (2 + 0.5*x - 0.0005*x^2), 5)
> > df <- data.frame(x=x, x2=x^2, y=y)
> > plot(y ~ x)
> >
> > # two models
> > library(inlabru)
> > m1 <- bru(y ~ 1 + x, data=df)
> > m2 <- bru(y ~ 1 + x + x2, data=df)
> >
> > # model weights
> > library(dplyr)
> > waics <- data.frame(model=c("m1", "m2"),
> >                         waic=c(m1$waic$waic, m2$waic$waic)) %>%
> >   arrange(waic) %>%
> >   mutate(delta_waic=waic-min(waic),
> >          rel_lik=round(exp(-0.5 * delta_waic), 3),
> >          waic_wts=rel_lik / sum(rel_lik)) %>%
> >   pull(waic_wts)
> >
> > # two sets of posteriors
> > fun1 = function() {return (Intercept + 50 * x)}
> > s1 <- inla.posterior.sample(50000, m1)
> > lc1 <- as.numeric(inla.posterior.sample.eval(fun1, s1)); summary(lc1); hist(lc1)
> >
> > fun2 = function() {return (Intercept + 50 * x + 50 * x2)}
> > s2 <- inla.posterior.sample(50000, m2)
> > lc2 <- as.numeric(inla.posterior.sample.eval(fun2, s2)); summary(lc2); hist(lc2)
> >
> > # weighted posterior
> > wt_post <- get_weighted_posterior(dists=list(lc1, lc2), wts=list(waics[1], waics[2]),
> >                        summa=T, histo=T)
> > wt_post$summaries

> Dear INLA experts,
>
> I have noticed that the parameters of my GLMM slightly change in value
> depending on whether I fit the model only to the observational data or
> if I include “testing” or “predicting” data points (i.e., the points
> of my regular grid). Here is what I mean:
>
> I fit my model like this:
>
> -----------------------------------
>
> MODS <- inla(formula = as.formula(FMLAS), data = hydrodata, family =
> "tweedie",
>           control.family = list(hyper =  list(
>               theta1 = list(initial = 1.725),
>               theta2 = list(initial = -4,
>                     prior = "loggamma",

>              verbose = T)

>
> where “hydrodata” contains only observations and my model FMLAS is:
>
> -----------------------------------
>
> > FMLAS

> TEMP:log(sumEP+1) + I(TEMP^2):log(sumEP+1) + log(sumEP+1) + LON + LAT

> this by appending the testing points to the data frame “hydrodata”

>                                 mean    sd 0.025quant 0.5quant

> 0.975quant

> 1.74

>  40.59
>
> -----------------------------------
>
> Here are my questions:
>
> 1) Why do the model parameter values change with the “predicting”
> data? For me this makes no sense, since a prediction should be
> independent of the data used to train the model... Is this dependence
> of model parameters on the predicting data with INLA correct at all or
> I am doing or understanding something wrong? In case this is correct,
> is this some kind of “Bayesian” standard issue, i.e., kind of a
> concept which does not exist in frequentist statistics?
>
> 2) I wonder if it is at all needed to involve the predicting points in
> the INLA fitting procedure. Why not simply to make a prediction by
> fitting the model only to the observations and, once the model
> parameters have been found, *evaluating* the GLM in the predicting
> points?
>
> Example of what I mean:
>
> -----------------------------------
>
> # Extract the model parameter values:
> modparam <- MODS$summary.fixed$mean
>
> # We need now to calculate the “model matrix”, but first,
> # we need to indicate R to include NAs in the predictors to obtain
> # also Nas in the model matrix (otherwise the model matrix is shorter
> # in the missing values):
> options(na.action='na.pass')
>
> # Now here comes the model matrix, i.e., a matrix including a column
> per model
> # term (including a column of 1s for the intercept) and each row being
> the
> # model term evaluated in a testing point of “climdata”:
> X0 <- model.matrix(as.formula(FMLAS), data = climdata)
>
> # We have to mutiply now the model matrix X0 with the vector of model
> # parameter values “modparam” *columnwise*. To do so, we define a
> # matrix with the values of modparam in the diagonal and use the
> # matrix multiplication operator %*% :
> AB_ <- X0 %*% diag(modparam)
>
> # Finally, we add the multiplication AB_ of fitted model
> # parameters and model terms evaluated on the testing points and apply
> # the inverse link function (in my case, it is a log link):
> AB <- exp(as.vector(rowSums(AB_)))
>
> -----------------------------------
>
> Now we have the predicted response stored the variable AB, evaluated
> on a regular grid. This procedure is identical to what you obtain with
> the function gam() of mgcv and the function predict(). You can even
> compute error estimates for the response variable by using the 0.95
> credible intervals instead of using the parameter means, i.e. repeat
> the procedure with:
>
> -----------------------------------
> modparam_high <- MODS$summary.fixed$"0.975quant"
>
> modparam_low <- MODS$summary.fixed$"0.025quant"
> -----------------------------------
>
> So, why not to use this “evaluation” procedure instead of including
> the predicting points in the call to inla()? Does it have any
> disadvantage in comparison? Is this only possible in the absence of
> random effects? Otherwise:
>
> How to do the “evaluation” procedure when you have random effects? I
> guess that you can extract the random parameters with
> MODS$summary.random but: is there also an equivalent “model matrix”
> for random effects? How to compute it?

messages.subject: Reference request: Extending R-INLA for 3D regullar lattice data
messages.subject_clean: Reference request: Extending R-INLA for 3D regullar lattice data
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

For my master's thesis I am working to implement several spatial models for fMRI data in R-INLA. The data contains only a single time step, corresponding to a summary of all temporal slices. I am currently working with the subcortical regions, which can be considered as a three-dimensional regullar latice. Each participant's data is stored as vector of length 30.000 x 1 containing the BOLD signal / acitivation amplitudes.

Yesterday I created a TsparseMatrix-class adjacency matrix based on the voxel coordinates to push the adjacent neighbors to the inla()-function. This seems to be accepted by the function. Now I am trying to figure out how to send all the data of the 1000 participants to the inla-function.

Are there any references you are aware of on how to work with 3D data for multiple subjects? I found many resources on 2D problems, and on how the SPDE approach can be used together with mesh structures. However, as I have regular lattice data, the SPDE approach seems unfeasible / unnecesarily complex. I also found papers on Bayesian spatial modeling for fMRI data, but the accompanying code isn't very transparent, and is largely adopted for cortical surface fMRI.

Any help is greatly appreciated.

Best,

Bas

messages.subject: Concurvity
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

Let f(x) be the spatial term in the model, and f(d) is another term I want to estimate. Now suppose d is a function of x.

In the world of GAMs (mgcv), if I try to estimate f(x) and f(d) in a model, those terms would be concurved. This makes estimation of the smoothing parameters potentially unstable and problematic for inference.

In the setting of R-INLA, are there potential problems with estimating two model terms that may potentially be concurved in the sense above? To be concrete, I will model f(x) with an SPDE model, and f(d) with a RW2 model.

Best,

W

messages.body_plain:
the problems of this type will not go away, but priors will make it more
'stable'

here is a small example (from your description), you'll see the fit is
good although the marginal uncertainty in each component is huge (which
is a sign that something is going on)

n <- 100
x <- (1:n)/n
f1 <- x+sin(10*x)
f2 <- exp(f1)
s <- 0.01
y <- f1 + f2 + rnorm(n, sd = s)

r <- inla(y ~ 1 + f(x, model = "rw2") + f(xx, model = "rw2"),
          data = data.frame(x = x, xx = x, y = y),
          control.family = list(
              hyper = list(prec = list(initial = log(1/s^2),
                                       fixed = TRUE))),
          verbose = TRUE)

On Tuesday, December 14, 2021 at 5:40:33 PM UTC+2 finn.l...@gmail.com wrote:
> Hi Shauhin,
>
> the rw1 process is non-differentiable, so it would only make sense to do this with e.g. rw2 models, where the derivative is well defined.
> Even though the posterior mean might look smooth, the joint distribution reveals that the realisations themselves aren't, and if you were to compute the finite difference "derivative estimate" posteriors you'd see that their variance will go to infinity the shorter the delta-value is.  This is in stark contrast to frequentist penalised spline point estimates, that have more in common with the posterior mean (or mode) than the actual posterior process distributions.
>
> That said, you can use the same approach as in other systems (if you have rw2 models). Likely easiest to use posterior sampling with inla.posterior.sample and calculate the finite differences for each sampled process.
>
> Finn

messages.subject_clean: how to calculate variance spatiotemporal modelling
messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA community,

I have fitted a spatiotemporal type 4 interaction model along with covariates. I would like to calculate the contribution of variance due to fixed effects and random effects. I have used the following code for calculating variance of different random components. Kindly advise me if my calculations are correct.

rm(list = ls())
library(spdep); library(INLA); library(tmap);library('sf');library("rgdal");library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)

#Calculate variance proportions
load("d:\\VL model_2\\vicente_52_models\\Modified_data_covariate_avg\\Output_E_base\\models with covariates\\bym2_rw1_t4_cov_training 2013-2018_20 may 2022.RData")

marg_hyper_bym2.rw1.t4= inla.hyperpar.sample(100000,model_bym2.rw1.t4)

var_prop = tibble(`Random Effects Term` = c("Unstructured Spatial",
                                            "Structured Spatial",
                                            "Unstructured Temporal",
                                            "Structured Temporal",
                                            "Space-Time Interaction"),

                  `bym2.rw1.t4 With Interaction` = c(mean(1/marg_hyper_bym2.rw1.t4[,1]/(1/marg_hyper_bym2.rw1.t4[,1]+1/marg_hyper_bym2.rw1.t4[,2]+1/marg_hyper_bym2.rw1.t4[,3]+1/marg_hyper_bym2.rw1.t4[,4]+1/marg_hyper_bym2.rw1.t4[,5])),
                                                     mean(1/marg_hyper_bym2.rw1.t4[,2]/(1/marg_hyper_bym2.rw1.t4[,1]+1/marg_hyper_bym2.rw1.t4[,2]+1/marg_hyper_bym2.rw1.t4[,3]+1/marg_hyper_bym2.rw1.t4[,4]+1/marg_hyper_bym2.rw1.t4[,5])),
                                                     mean(1/marg_hyper_bym2.rw1.t4[,3]/(1/marg_hyper_bym2.rw1.t4[,1]+1/marg_hyper_bym2.rw1.t4[,2]+1/marg_hyper_bym2.rw1.t4[,3]+1/marg_hyper_bym2.rw1.t4[,4]+1/marg_hyper_bym2.rw1.t4[,5])),
                                                     mean(1/marg_hyper_bym2.rw1.t4[,4]/(1/marg_hyper_bym2.rw1.t4[,1]+1/marg_hyper_bym2.rw1.t4[,2]+1/marg_hyper_bym2.rw1.t4[,3]+1/marg_hyper_bym2.rw1.t4[,4]+1/marg_hyper_bym2.rw1.t4[,5])),
                                                     mean(1/marg_hyper_bym2.rw1.t4[,5]/(1/marg_hyper_bym2.rw1.t4[,1]+1/marg_hyper_bym2.rw1.t4[,2]+1/marg_hyper_bym2.rw1.t4[,3]+1/marg_hyper_bym2.rw1.t4[,4]+1/marg_hyper_bym2.rw1.t4[,5]))))

var_prop = var_prop %>%
  mutate(`bym2_rw1.t4 ` = round(`bym2.rw1.t4 With Interaction`*100,3),
         `bym2.rw1.t4` = round(`bym2.rw1.t4 With Interaction`*100,3))

Also I would appreciate your advise on how to calculate the overall variance of (i) fixed effects and (ii) random effects.

Thanks in advance
ssubra

messages.subject: Validation of ZANB model with random effect
messages.subject_clean: Validation of ZANB model with random effect
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am trying to validate a ZANB model with random factor (ID) for count data with excess of zeros.

Following Zuur (2017), before to combine them I’ve got the posterior mean values for each model: 1) mod01(Bernoulli for presence/absence data)  and 2) mod.pos (truncated negative binomial model for non-zero data). But I’ve got error message (it can’t find ID). Could you help me to identify the error? How do I have to include the random component in the code?

Below I copy the code

---------------------------------

X <- model.matrix(~ var1 + var2 + var3, data = data) #covariate matrix

X <- as.matrix(X)

Beta01 <- mod01$summary.fixed[, "mean"]

r01 <- mod01$summary.random$ID$mean

Pi <- exp(X %*% Beta01 + ID %*% r01)/(1 + exp(X %*% Bet01 + ID %*% r01))

Beta.Pos <- mod.pos$summary.fixed[, "mean"]

rPos <- mod.pos$summary.random$ID$mean

k       <- mod.pos$summary.hyper[1,"mean"]

mu <- exp(X %*% Beta.Pos + ID %*% rPos)

P0 <- (k / (mu + k))^k

muZANB <- (Pi / (1 - P0))  * mu

varZANB <- (Pi / (1 - P0)) * (mu^2 + mu + mu^2 / k ) - (Pi / (1 - P0) * mu)^2

Thank you in advance for your help

Regards

Barbara

I have searched up in the thread you mentioned (and some other relevant threads). I have looked at that thread before, but I guess my question is about what exactly is the standard/correct way of fitting such model (separate covariate model for both the binary part and continuous part). Thank you so much.

Best,
Jocelyn

messages.subject: Re: Smoothers with interactions - coding issue
messages.body_plain:
Hi Suzanne,

If you are looking to have a separate smooth per site, consider the 'group' and 'replicate' options for the rw2 effects: https://groups.google.com/g/r-inla-discussion-group/c/W4nTB8h1ZAY/m/31D3FaTpAgAJ

Best,
Tim

On Tuesday, January 24, 2023 at 6:14:57 AM UTC-7 suuz...@gmail.com wrote:
> Hello,
>
> I am trying to run a ZIP model in inla that has smoothers with interactions (e.g. smoother for week of year that has an interaction with site).
>
> The model below is crashing. I've tried with a subset to check its not a memory issue.
>
> I've also built the model step by step, so have a working model that includes inetractions but no smoothers, and another that has smoothers but no interactions. It seems to be this next step to smoothers with interactions that is causing the issue so perhaps it is my coding?
>
> Any advice would be much apprecaited,
> Suzanne
>
>
> f5 <- hpDPM ~ TimeLost.std + Angle.std + Nall.std + dolDPM.std + dist.std + Serial + Year*Site +
>   f(woy.std, Site,  model = "rw2", cyclic=TRUE, hyper = hyper.prec) +
>   f(Sdiel.std, Site, model = "rw2", cyclic=TRUE, hyper = hyper.prec)
>
> I5 <- inla(f5,  control.predictor = list(  compute = TRUE,
>   quantiles = c(0.025, 0.975)),
>   control.compute = list(config = TRUE,dic = TRUE),
>   family = "zeroinflatedpoisson0",
>   data = dat, verbose=TRUE, control.inla = list(int.strategy="eb"))
>
>
messages.body_snippet:
Hi Suzanne,

If you are looking to have a separate smooth per site, consider the 'group' and 'replicate' options for the rw2 effects: https://groups.google.com/g/r-inla-discussion-group/c/W4nTB8h1ZAY/

messages.subject: Stochastic Gompertz state space model
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am trying to get some state space models running in INLA. So far I have a stochastic level (random walk with noise) model going and a stochastic level with drift (random walk with drift) model going. I am trying to take it one more step to get a stochastic Gompertz model running but can't figure it out. Any help is appreciated. Code is below.

Thanks, Tim

#### libraries
library(INLA); library(brinla)

#### make and plot data
n = 50; m <- n-1; x0 = 20
W = 0.3; V = 0.3;
d0 = 5; d1 = -0.3
w  = rnorm(n, 0, W); v  = rnorm(n, 0, V)
x = y = rep(0, n)
x[1] = x0 + w[1]
y[1] = x[1] +       v[1]
for (t in 2:n){
  x[t] = x[t-1] + d0 + d1*x[t-1] + w[t]
  y[t] = x[t]   +         v[t]
}
plot(y,type="l",xlab="time",ylab=""); lines(x,col=2)
legend("topright",legend=c("y","x"), col=c("black", "red"),
       lty=c(1,1), bty="n")

#### create y matrix for augmented model
Y <- matrix(NA, n+m, 2)
Y[1:n,     1] <- y
Y[1:m + n, 2] <- 0

#### indices and weights
i  <- c(1:n, 2:n)              # indices for  the states x_t
j  <- c(rep(NA,n), 2:n -1)     # indices for x_{t-1}
wj <- c(rep(NA,n), rep(-1,m))  # weights for x_{t-1}
l  <- c(rep(NA,n), 2:n)        # indices for the perturbation terms w_t
wl <- c(rep(NA,n), rep(-1,m))  # weights for w_t
d0 <- c(rep(NA,n), rep(-1,m))  # constant drift

#### stochastic level model
# x_t = x_{t-1} + w_t         where w_t ~ N(0, W)
# 0 = x_t - x_{t-1} - w_t     where w_t ~ N(0, W)
formula1 <- Y ~ -1 +
  f(i, model="iid", initial=-10, fixed=T) + # x_t
  f(j, wj, copy="i") + # x_{t-1}
  f(l, wl, model ="iid") # perterbations w_t
r1 <- inla(formula1, data = data.frame(i, j, wj, l, wl, d0),
           family = rep("gaussian", 2),
           control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE),
           control.compute = list(waic=T))
summary(r1)
bri.hyperpar.summary(r1)
plot(y); lines(r1$summary.random$i$mean)
r1$waic$waic

#### stochastic level with drift, d0, model
# x_t = x_{t-1} + d0 + w_t        where w_t ~ N(0, W)
# 0 = x_t - x_{t-1} - d0 - w_t    where w_t ~ N(0, W)
formula2 <- Y ~ -1 +
  f(i, model="iid", initial=-10, fixed=T) + # x_t
  f(j, wj, copy="i") + # x_{t-1}
  f(l, wl, model ="iid") + # perterbations w_t
  d0 # drift constant?
r2 <- inla(formula2, data = data.frame(i, j, wj, wl, l, d0),
           family = rep("gaussian", 2),
           control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE),
           control.compute = list(waic=T))
summary(r2)
bri.hyperpar.summary(r2)
plot(y); lines(r2$summary.random$i$mean)
r2$waic$waic

#### stochastic gompertz with baseline growth, d0, and growth penalty, d1
# x_t = x_{t-1} + d0 + d1*x_{t-1} + w_t       where w_t ~ N(0, W)
# 0 = x_t - x_{t-1} - d0 - d1*x_{t-1} - w_t     where w_t ~ N(0, W)

# additional indices or weights?
k <-
wk <-

# new formula?
formula3 <- Y ~ -1 +

# compute?
r3 <- inla(formula3, data = data.frame(i, j, wj, wl, l, d0), # add more inputs?
           family = rep("gaussian", 2),
           control.predictor=list(compute=TRUE),
           control.compute = list(waic=T))

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Stochastic Gompertz state space model
messages.body_plain:
you can have more than one copy (of the same effect) in the formula

f(time,...) +
f(time1, w.neg.one, copy="time") +
f(time2, w.neg.one, copy="time",
	hyper=list(beta=list(fixed=FALSE))  ## to get 'd1'

assuming t=1...n, then

time=1:n
time1=c(NA, 1:(n-1))
time2=time1
w.neg.one=rep(-1,n)

but you can also join x_{t-1} and d1*x_{t-1} if you like, even if you
know the sign of 'd1', as you can define an interval for the scaling in
copy via  range=c(low,high) argument,

   range: A vector of size two giving the lower and upper range for the
          scaling parameter ‘beta’ in the model ‘COPY’, ‘CLINEAR’,
          ‘MEC’ and ‘MEB’. If ‘low = high’ then the identity mapping is
          used.

> # 0 = x_t - x_{t-1} - d0 - d1*x_{t-1} - w_t     where w_t ~ N(0, W)

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Stochastic Gompertz state space model
messages.body_plain:
x_t can only be indexed from 2 to 50, and x_{t-1} from 1 to 49.
If you want to directly involve x_1 you'll need to work out some kind
of "initial distribution" for that; for stationary AR(1) processes
without drift that's well defined (and what INLA does internally), but
when you have drift there's no clear "right way".
The easiest solution is to not involve that in the likelihood, and
instead only involve the fully defined pairs.

Finn

messages.subject: instability with cloglog link
messages.body_plain:
Hi, I'm fitting a cloglog linked model, but finding lots of errors and fitted values all near 1. Fitting with a logit link works fine. A reproducible example is below. The usual tricks of using EB, large diagonal, and refitting haven't worked in my real-world example, though adding a stronger prior on the random effects and then re-fitting without that prior produces reasonable results...though I'm having a hard time replicating that in an example to share.

It makes me suspect that an optimizer is getting stuck somewhere, though it is pure speculation on my part... I don't know how the cloglog link is represented internally, and whether cancellation of log's and exp's is used in the log likelihood for binomial models, but that as a source of numerical instability struck me as a possible issue looking at inla.link.invcloglog(x).

##
library(INLA)
library(tidyverse)
set.seed(2)
#10 samples from each of 100 sites
n <- 100
m <- 10
df <- expand_grid(site_id = 1:n, sample_id = 1:m) %>%
    mutate(
        site_effect = rnorm(n, 0, 1)[site_id],
        sample_effect = rnorm(nrow(.), -4, 1.5),
        eta = 2 + site_effect + sample_effect,
        mu = binomial('cloglog')$linkinv(eta),
        N = 1,
        y = rbinom(nrow(.), N, mu)
    )
#fails, restarts, and ends up with wild estimates for site_id precision:
mod_cloglog <- inla(y ~ f(site_id) + offset(sample_effect),
    N = N,
    family = "binomial",
    control.family = list(link = "cloglog"),
    data = df
)
mod_cloglog$summary.hyperpar

#fitted values are all nearly 1:
mod_cloglog$summary.fitted.values$mean %>% summary()

#logit seems to work fine:
mod_logit <- inla(y ~ f(site_id) + offset(sample_effect),
    N = N,
    family = "binomial",
    control.family = list(link = "logit"),
    data = df
)
mod_logit$summary.hyperpar

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Reproducibility for INLA fitted value
messages.body_plain:
My experience, at least at the moment, is more positive.

With a binomial model, which perhaps does involve (?) some random simulation in the conversion from the linear predictor on the link function back to the actual fitted values on the original scale, if that prediction option is selected, you will get slightly different values each time if you set no seed before you run the same model, but will get the same values each time to a great many decimal places if you set the same seed right before the model is run and proceed to run it multiple times, even if you are running it in parallel.  Perhaps this particular model (with a few iid effects and fixed effects) is just simpler but I would consider this to be excellent reproducibility for a fitted value, whatever its underlying cause.

> On Wednesday, May 12, 2021 at 6:03:46 PM UTC+2 finn.l...@gmail.com wrote:
> > The R random seed is essentially irrelevant for regular inla() runs, as it doesn't do MCMC. The differences you see are most likely due to numerical fluctuations due to order of operations in the parallel computations.
> > Normally, these fluctuations are negligible, but it means that, as nearly always when floating point computations are involved, and doubly when parallel computations are involved, exact equality should be expected.
> >
> > For debugging purposes, you can use num.threads="1:1" to force single-threaded calculations, which normally does produce the exact same values each time, but for "production use", it's better to handle the floating point values appropriately instead (i.e., to not expect them to be exactly equal).
> >
> > Finn
> >

messages.subject_clean: problems with fitted errors in space time models
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I am kindly asking for your help.:)

My problem setup is the following:  I have 56 measurement stations for rain over 12 month and I look at the aggregated monthly values (total of 672 space time data), so I built the observation matrix and my index as:

A.est<-inla.spde.make.A(mesh, loc=coords,group=monthly.value$Time,n.group = month)
and
index<-inla.spde.make.index("field", n.spde=spde$n.spde, n.group=month)

I know that rain is in general gamma distributed, but I transform it via log(rain) to a gauss distribution.

My formula is then:
formula<-log(rain)~-1+Intercept+f(field,model=spde,group=field.group, control.group = list(model="ar1"))
And I perform INLA (where my stack consists of observation data; no prediction stack so far).

Then I project my spatial field to a grid and get a projection of the random field for every time step by
inla.mesh.project( projgrid, result$summary.random$field$mean[index$field.group == j])
(Please correct me but this is not on the log-scale as I only transformed my response to log-scale right? :) )

Then I continue to get the expected precipitation: I get 14272 pred.points within my area of interest, build a prediction stack, combine it with the estimation stack, and run INLA again. But now, I am struggeling to plot my expected rain  for each of my 12 month. Do you have any idea if I can fix this problem?

And now I need to back transform from the log-scale for sure but for the standard deviation it is not just the exponent(sd) right?

I am so much looking forward to your help.

All the best,
Corinna

Alessandro

I would guess so. I presume you have Linux on the VM, then register for
the PARDISO library, with

	inla.pardiso()

its all there already, you just need to activate it.

make sure you have R-4.2 and the most recent testing version

if H is the number of hyperparametes, then set

	num.threads="A:B"

where A=2*H+1 or 2*H, and B=1 or 2

if its still slow, send data/code so i can recheck here

Best
H

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] problems with fitted errors in space time models
messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] problems with fitted errors in space time models
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

If you have included all the terms in the prediction stack, you can take the summary.fitted.values and use it considering that it is the summary of the posterior marginal distributions for E(log(y)) at each one of the 14272 points (use the inla.stack.index() function to get the right 14272 elements).

The sd column in the summary.fitted.values is the standard error of the expected value of the logarithm of y, SD(E(log(y))), and is not not SD(log(y)). To have SD(log(y)) you need to account for the precision of the likelihood, or the error after the linear predictor.

The easiest way to have SD(y) is considering Monte Carlo samples from the joint posterior. Then use these samples to have samples from y at each prediction point. This is easier if you consider inlabru this is a lot easier, as you can see from this tutorial https://inlabru-org.github.io/inlabru/articles/web/random_fields_2d.html

best regards,
Elias

> and

>
> I know that rain is in general gamma distributed, but I transform it via log(rain) to a gauss distribution.
>
> My formula is then:
> formula<-log(rain)~-1+Intercept+f(field,model=spde,group=field.group, control.group = list(model="ar1"))
> And I perform INLA (where my stack consists of observation data; no prediction stack so far).
>
> Then I project my spatial field to a grid and get a projection of the random field for every time step by
> inla.mesh.project( projgrid, result$summary.random$field$mean[index$field.group == j])
> (Please correct me but this is not on the log-scale as I only transformed my response to log-scale right? :) )

> Then I continue to get the expected precipitation: I get 14272 pred.points within my area of interest, build a prediction stack, combine it with the estimation stack, and run INLA again. But now, I am struggeling to plot my expected rain  for each of my 12 month. Do you have any idea if I can fix this problem?
>
> And now I need to back transform from the log-scale for sure but for the standard deviation it is not just the exponent(sd) right?

> I am so much looking forward to your help.
